intro: Every match has a start. In a judo room, players bow. In a wrestling room, they shake hands. In a boxing ring, a bell rings. In a school gym, a whistle blows.
Each signal has a history. It comes from a place and a people. Old paintings, books and records help us learn these stories.
In this unit, you will name the signals different rooms use. You will learn where they come from. You will tell a legend apart from a record.
bigQuestion: How do people start a match fairly, and how do we learn where those ways came from?

title: Fair Start

chapters.title: Bow, Handshake, Whistle
chapters.bigQuestion: How do different rooms show that a match is about to start?

story.title: Two Rooms, One Minute
story.kicker: Two classes start at the same time, with two different signals.
paragraphs: It is nine o'clock. In the school gym, a PE teacher lifts a whistle. She blows one short sound. The children stop and look up. Class has begun.
Across town, a judo class starts at nine o'clock too. There is no whistle. The students kneel in a line on the mat. They bow to their teacher, and the teacher bows back.
Both rooms began at the same minute. One used a sound. One used a bow. Each signal tells people the same thing: now we start, and the rules are on.
People around the world start matches in many ways. Fencers salute. Wrestlers shake hands. Boxers wait for a bell. Each room has its own signal and its own history.
story.think: What signal tells you that your class has started?

lessons.title: The Judo Bow
lessons.mainIdea: In judo, people bow when they enter the room and before a match.
reading: Judo began in Tokyo, Japan. A teacher named Kano Jigoro started his school in 1882. He called the school the Kodokan.
In many judo schools, students *bow* when they step onto the mat. Two players bow to each other before a match. They bow again at the end.
In Japan, a bow is a common way to say hello and thank you. Judo schools kept this everyday sign of respect.

words.d: bending forward to show respect; it is a common greeting in Japan
the judo school Kano Jigoro started in Tokyo in 1882

lessons.title: Sumo Starts Together
lessons.mainIdea: In sumo, there is no whistle; the two wrestlers start at the same moment.
reading: Before a sumo match, wrestlers stand in the ring. Many toss a handful of salt. This custom comes from Shinto, an old religion of Japan. In Shinto, salt stands for making a place clean.
A *referee* in a bright robe watches. He holds a wooden fan. The two wrestlers crouch and face each other. They choose the moment to start together. This start is called the *tachiai*.

words.d: the person who watches a match and makes sure the rules are kept
the moment two sumo wrestlers start a match together

lessons.title: The Fencing Salute
lessons.mainIdea: Fencers salute each other and the referee before a bout.
reading: *Fencing* is a sport with long, thin swords. It grew from sword schools in Europe. Fencing has been in every modern Olympics since 1896.
Before a bout, each fencer gives a *salute*. They salute the other fencer and the referee. The rule book of world fencing asks for it. A fencer who will not salute can be punished.

words.d: a sport with thin swords that grew from sword schools in Europe
a sign of respect given before a match

check.q: Since when has fencing been in every modern Olympics?
check.why: Fencing has been in every modern Olympics since the first one in 1896.

lessons.title: A Handshake on the Mat
lessons.mainIdea: Wrestlers shake hands before and after a match.
reading: Wrestling is one of the oldest sports in the world. Today, a world group called United World Wrestling writes its rules.
Before a match, the two wrestlers meet in the middle. They *shake hands*. After the match, they shake hands again. Then they shake hands with the other coach too.
In the United States, school wrestlers shake hands too. The handshake says, we both agree to the rules.

words.d: to hold another person's hand as a greeting or a promise
the world group that writes the rules for Olympic wrestling

lessons.title: The Boxing Bell
lessons.mainIdea: In boxing, a bell starts and ends each round.
reading: Boxing matches are cut into parts called *rounds*. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 made each round three minutes long. A rest of one minute came between rounds.
A person called the timekeeper watches the clock. The timekeeper rings a *bell*. One ring starts the round. Another ring ends it. Everyone in the room can hear it.

words.d: one timed part of a boxing match
the sound that starts and ends each round in boxing

lessons.title: The Whistle in the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: In a school gym, a whistle is a common signal to start and stop.
reading: Many PE teachers and referees use a *whistle*. Its sound is short and loud. It can be heard across a big room.
In 1884, a toolmaker named Joseph Hudson made a famous whistle in Birmingham, England. He called it the Acme Thunderer. Referees around the world used it.

words.d: a small tool that makes a loud, high sound when you blow into it
a sound or sign that tells people what to do

lessons.title: Honoring the Teacher
lessons.mainIdea: In Muay Thai, fighters often honor their teachers before a match.
reading: *Muay Thai* comes from Thailand. Before a match, many fighters do the *wai khru*. Wai khru means paying respect to the teacher in Thai.
The fighter moves slowly around the ring while music plays. Each gym has its own way. People who watch can learn what it means. It belongs to the fighter and the gym.

words.d: a fighting sport from Thailand
a Muay Thai custom of paying respect to teachers before a match

chapters.title: Finding the Old Stories
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we know what matches were like long ago?

story.title: A New Book on the Table
story.kicker: A teacher opens a book full of old pictures and old rules.
paragraphs: It is reading time. A teacher opens a big book on the rug. The first page shows a painting on a stone wall. Two wrestlers reach for each other.
The painting is about four thousand years old. It comes from a tomb in Egypt. The children lean in close. How can a picture last so long?
The next page shows an old rule book. Then a photo of a museum in Tokyo. Each page holds a clue about the past. The children count three kinds of clues.
History is like a puzzle. Pictures, books, records and places are the pieces. People who study history put the pieces together.
story.think: What old thing in your home could tell a story about the past?

lessons.title: Wrestlers on a Tomb Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Paintings in Egyptian tombs show that wrestling is very old.
reading: Beni Hasan is a place in Egypt, near the Nile River. People carved tombs into the cliffs there about four thousand years ago.
Painters covered the tomb walls with pictures. One wall shows many pairs of *wrestlers*. Each pair is shown in a different pose.
These *paintings* are clues. They tell us people in Egypt wrestled long, long ago.

words.d: people who take part in wrestling
pictures made with paint; old ones are clues about the past

look.title: Rows on a Wall
look.text: Look at a long stone wall inside a cliff. Rows of small painted people cover it. In each row, two people hold on to each other. The paint is red, brown and black.
look.prompt: What can a picture tell us, even when no one wrote words?

check.why: The tombs were made about four thousand years ago.

lessons.title: Pictures on Greek Pots
lessons.mainIdea: Old Greek pots show wrestling and boxing at the ancient games.
reading: Long ago, people in Greece held games at a place called Olympia. These were the *ancient Olympics*. They were held every four years.
Greek writers said wrestling joined the games in 708 BCE. Boxing joined in 688 BCE. Artists painted these sports on clay *pots*. Many of those pots are in museums today.

words.d: the old games held at Olympia in Greece every four years
clay jars; Greek pots often had paintings on them

lessons.title: Kano Writes It Down
lessons.mainIdea: Kano Jigoro wrote down his ideas, so we can read how judo began.
reading: Kano Jigoro started judo in 1882. He was also a school teacher. He wrote many talks and articles about judo.
He wrote about two big ideas. One means best use of energy. The other means helping each other so all do well. Judo schools still teach these *ideas*.
Because Kano *wrote* things down, we can read his own words today. Judo teachers in many countries still read them.

words.d: put words on paper so others could read them later

lessons.title: Olympic Records
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic records tell us the year each sport joined the modern games.
reading: The *International Olympic Committee* keeps careful lists. They show which sports were in each Olympics. These lists are called *records*.
The records show that judo joined in 1964, in Tokyo. Women's judo joined in 1992, in Barcelona. Taekwondo joined in 2000, in Sydney.

words.d: careful written lists of what happened and when

lessons.title: A Legend in an Old Book
lessons.mainIdea: An old book from Japan tells a sumo legend, a story we cannot prove.
reading: The Nihon Shoki is an old book of Japan. It was finished in the year 720. It tells a story about two strong men in a match.
Many people call this the first sumo match. But it is a *legend*. A legend is an old story that no one can prove. *Historians* keep legends and proof apart.

words.d: an old story that is told again and again but cannot be proved
people who study the past and check the clues

lessons.title: Museums in Tokyo
lessons.mainIdea: Museums keep old objects so people can learn from them.
reading: A *museum* is a place that keeps old things safe. People visit to look and learn.
In Tokyo, the big sumo hall has a Sumo Museum. It keeps old prints, belts and banners. The Kodokan in Tokyo has a judo museum too. It tells the story of Kano and his school.

words.d: a place that keeps old or special objects safe for people to see
things you can see and touch, like belts, prints and pots
